title: Finding the Area of a Compound Shape by Adding Its Rectangular Parts
subject: Mathematics

nodes.text: **An L-shaped floor plan is made from two rectangles, so no single length-by-width pair describes the whole floor.** The top edge of the plan measures 8 m and the overall left edge measures 7 m, but the corner region at the bottom right of that outline is not part of the floor. Those two edges are therefore not the sides of one rectangle. Look instead at the two rectangular parts the floor is made of, and read the measurements marked along their sides.

nodes.caption: An L-shaped floor plan made from two rectangles, with the top edge labelled 8 m, the depth of the top rectangle labelled 3 m, the overall left vertical edge labelled 7 m, and the lower rectangle's width labelled 5 m. The bottom-right corner of the enclosing outline is not part of the floor.

nodes.text: You have seen that the floor is not a single rectangle. Before we deal with that, the area rule for one rectangle needs to be solid. **The area of a rectangle is its length times its width, reported in square units.** Area counts unit squares, so the result is a number of square units such as m^2^, not a length.

nodes.prompt: A single rectangle measures 6 m by 4 m. What is its area?

options.text: 24 m²

contract.prompt: A single rectangle measures 6 m by 4 m. What is its area?

options.text: 24 m²

shared_task.purpose: surface whether the rectangle rule and the square-unit convention are still available before the compound case is built on them
shared_task.prompt: A single rectangle measures 6 m by 4 m. What is its area?
shared_task.expected_evidence: the learner selects 24 m² rather than 10 m, 24 m, or 24 without a unit

options.text: 24 m²

nodes.title: A split must not overlap or leave gaps
nodes.belief: I can split a shape into rectangles, add their areas, and it doesn't matter if the pieces overlap or if a bit of the shape is left out.
nodes.evidence: Suppose two rectangles both cover the same middle strip. Adding their areas counts that strip twice, so the total is bigger than the shape really is. The same thing happens when a corner is left uncovered: that region is counted zero times.
nodes.conclusion: The parts must not overlap, and together they must cover the shape exactly, so every region is counted once and nothing is counted twice.

nodes.text:
**A single straight cut turns the L-shaped floor into two rectangles whose areas can be added.**

The cut runs across the full 8 m width, giving a top strip 8 m by 3 m and a lower rectangle 5 m wide. Its depth is the rest of the 7 m left edge: 7 m − 3 m = 4 m. The parts share only the cut line and cover the whole floor.

nodes.caption: The L-shaped floor plan with the single cut that separates the floor into two rectangles: the top rectangle running 8 m across and 3 m deep, and the lower rectangle 5 m wide with its depth obtained as 7 m − 3 m = 4 m.

nodes.label: Top strip, lower rectangle, and whole floor
nodes.condition: the two parts share only the cut line

nodes.caption: The floor plan split into the top rectangle and the lower rectangle, with the top rectangle carrying 24 m^2^ from 8 m × 3 m, the lower rectangle carrying 20 m^2^ from 5 m × 4 m, and the two part-areas added to give the whole floor, 44 m^2^.

nodes.title: Overall length times overall width
nodes.belief: I can find the floor's area by multiplying the overall length by the overall width: 8 m × 7 m = 56 m^2^.
nodes.evidence: But the floor is the two rectangles: 8 m × 3 m = 24 m^2^ and 5 m × 4 m = 20 m^2^, giving 24 m^2^ + 20 m^2^ = 44 m^2^. The extra 56 m^2^ − 44 m^2^ = 12 m^2^ is the 3 m by 4 m bottom-right region, not part of the floor.
nodes.conclusion: The floor's area is the two part-areas added: 24 m^2^ + 20 m^2^ = 44 m^2^. Multiplying the overall sides counts a 3 m by 4 m region outside the floor.

nodes.caption: The L-shaped floor plan with the enclosing 8 m by 7 m rectangle drawn around the floor and the 3 m by 4 m bottom-right region of that rectangle shaded as not part of the floor, showing 56 m^2^ compared with the correct 44 m^2^.

nodes.text: **To find a compound shape's area, split it into rectangles that do not overlap, multiply each part, then add.** The stage floor is a main rectangle 12 m by 5 m and an extension 2 m by 6 m, joined along an edge with nothing shared. Decide whether the parts overlap and whether any part is left uncovered, then find each part's area and the whole.

nodes.caption: A compound stage floor: a main rectangle labelled 12 m by 5 m and an extension rectangle labelled 2 m by 6 m, joined along an edge, with no shared region between the two rectangles.

nodes.prompt: A stage floor is made from a main rectangle 12 m by 5 m and an extension rectangle 2 m by 6 m joined along an edge, with nothing shared between the two parts. The split is shown. Work out the area of each part and then the area of the whole stage floor.

contract.prompt: A stage floor is made from a main rectangle 12 m by 5 m and an extension rectangle 2 m by 6 m joined along an edge, with nothing shared between the two parts. The split is shown. Work out the area of each part and then the area of the whole stage floor.

shared_task.purpose: rehearse the summing method with the split still supplied, so the learner reads the dimensions, multiplies and adds while the decomposition is scaffolded
shared_task.prompt: A stage floor is made from a main rectangle 12 m by 5 m and an extension rectangle 2 m by 6 m joined along an edge, with nothing shared between the two parts. The split is shown. Work out the area of each part and then the area of the whole stage floor.
shared_task.expected_evidence: 60 m² and 12 m² for the two parts and 72 m² for the whole stage floor

nodes.title: A split that overlaps
nodes.belief: Any split works. Once I have two parts, I just add their areas, even when the parts sit on top of one another.
nodes.evidence: Read as a 5 m by 7 m left column and an 8 m by 3 m top strip, the floor gives 35 m^2^ + 24 m^2^ = 59 m^2^. Those two parts share the top-left 5 m by 3 m region, so 15 m^2^ is counted twice.
nodes.conclusion: The parts of a split must not overlap, because every region of the shape has to be counted exactly once. The correct split gives 44 m^2^.

nodes.caption: The floor plan with a 5 m by 7 m left column and an 8 m by 3 m top strip drawn as the two proposed parts. The 5 m by 3 m region where they overlap is marked as the region counted twice, and 35 m^2^ + 24 m^2^ = 59 m^2^ is compared with the correct 44 m^2^.

nodes.text:
A common belief is that the unit is just decoration, so 44 on its own is enough. A bare 44 does not say what was counted, and it could just as well be a length of the room's edge. Area is a count of unit squares, so the floor's area is written 44 m^2^.

Every area answer needs its square units attached. Whatever total you reach for the stage floor, write it in m^2^, because the number alone does not tell a reader what was measured.

**This check shows whether you can choose the area method on your own.**

Here the shape is formed by joining two rectangles along an edge with no overlap. No split is drawn for you and no steps are suggested, so read each option and select the one that gives the area.

nodes.prompt: A compound shape is formed by joining a 7 cm by 2 cm rectangle and a 3 cm by 4 cm rectangle along an edge with no overlap. Which method gives the area?

options.text: Sum the areas of the two edge-joined rectangles
Multiply the overall length by the overall width of the joined shape
Count any shared edge region twice when adding the two rectangles
Report the total as 26 square units without naming the unit

option_notes.a: Correct: adds the areas of two non-overlapping rectangles joined along an edge.
option_notes.b: Misconception multiply_all_sides — treats the joined shape as one rectangle.
option_notes.c: Misconception overlap_double_count — adds a shared region more than once.
option_notes.d: Misconception forget_square_units — drops the square-unit label.
